parts: In this poem David Roth describes a hundred-yard race at the Special Olympics. When the smallest runner falls, the other eight turn back to help him, and all nine finish together holding hands. The poem shows that human values such as empathy, cooperation and kindness are more important than winning.

Athletes have come from all over the country to run for gold, silver and bronze after many weeks and months of training. Spectators gather around the old field to cheer the young men and women; the final event of the day — the hundred-yard dash — is approaching, and excitement grows.

Nine determined ('resolved') athletes stand behind the starting line, poised for the sound of the gun. The pistol explodes and the runners charge ahead, but the smallest among them stumbles, staggers and falls to the asphalt. He cries out in frustration and anguish; his dreams and efforts are 'dashed in the dirt'.

Then something wonderful happens: the eight other runners, who had trained so long to compete, pull up on their heels, turn around one by one, go back and bring the young boy to his feet. All nine join hands and continue; the dash becomes a walk. The banner above saying 'Special Olympics' could not have been 'more on the mark' (more fitting).
The race ends with nine gold medals: they reach the finish line still holding hands, to a standing ovation, and their nine beaming faces 'said more than these words ever will'.

Winning is not everything; compassion, sharing and togetherness make everyone a winner. Sport teaches cooperation as well as competition. The title shows that all nine deserved gold for their humanity. Devices: alliteration ('stumbled and staggered'), metaphor ('dreams… dashed in the dirt'), word pairs ('frustration and anguish'), and a narrative, conversational style.
Special Olympics is an international organisation, founded by Eunice Shriver, that helps people with intellectual disabilities build confidence and social skills through sport.
